title: Splitting a bounded finite-free complex with projective cohomology
statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $L^\bullet$ be a bounded cochain complex of finite free $R$-modules (having a finite basis, as in [def-weil-pbc-free-module]), with cohomology $H^i(L)=\ker(d^i)/\operatorname{im}(d^{i-1})$, viewed in the derived category $D(R)$ of [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. If every $H^i(L)$ is a projective $R$-module [def-weil-pbc-projective-module], then in $D(R)$ there is an isomorphism

$$L\simeq\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbf Z}H^i(L)[-i],$$

where only finitely many summands are nonzero. More precisely, writing $B^{i}=\operatorname{im}(d^{i-1})$, the complex $L^\bullet$ is isomorphic, as a complex, to the direct sum of the complexes $H^i(L)[-i]$ (zero differential) and of the two-term complexes $B^{i+1}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}B^{i+1}$ placed in degrees $i,i+1$, and the latter are contractible, meaning that their identity chain maps have the form $dh+hd$ for degree $-1$ maps $h$.

source.place: paragraph beginning ‘We record the elementary splitting argument needed here’

proof.text: Choose integers $a\leq b$ with $L^i=0$ outside $[a,b]$. Put $Z^i=\ker d^i$ and $B^i=\operatorname{im}d^{i-1}$. Since $d^id^{i-1}=0$, $B^i\subseteq Z^i$. The corestriction $p_i:L^i\to B^{i+1}$ of $d^i$ is surjective with kernel $Z^i$, and the quotient $q_i:Z^i\to H^i(L)$ is surjective with kernel $B^i$. These assertions follow directly from image, kernel, and quotient. In particular $B^{b+1}=0$ and $Z^i=B^i=H^i(L)=0$ for $i$ outside $[a,b]$.

source.place: paragraph beginning ‘We record the elementary splitting argument needed here’

proof.text: Use the lifting characterization of projectivity in [def-weil-pbc-projective-module]. Every $L^i$ is projective: its basis gives a free module, which is a direct summand of itself using the identity maps. Zero is projective by the same characterization, using the free module with empty basis. We will also use the following immediate lifting argument. If $j:P\to M$ and $r:M\to P$ satisfy $rj=1_P$ and $M$ is projective, then for a surjection $u:U\to V$ and a map $f:P\to V$, lift $fr$ to $g:M\to U$; the map $gj$ lifts $f$. Thus every retract of a projective module is projective. This is the only closure property of projectives used below.

source.place: Tags 05CE and 05CF, definition-projective and lemma-characterize-projective; direct summands and lifting

proof.text:
For the descending induction, suppose $B^{i+1}$ is projective. Lift $1_{B^{i+1}}$ along the surjection $p_i:L^i\to B^{i+1}$ using [def-weil-pbc-projective-module], obtaining $t_i:B^{i+1}\to L^i$ with $p_it_i=1$. For $x\in L^i$, $x-t_ip_i(x)$ lies in $Z^i$. The mutually inverse maps
$$Z^i\oplus B^{i+1}\longrightarrow L^i,\quad(z,c)\longmapsto z+t_i(c),\qquad x\longmapsto(x-t_ip_i(x),p_i(x))$$
give a splitting. In particular $Z^i$ is a retract of $L^i$, so is projective by step 2.

source.place: paragraph beginning ‘We record the elementary splitting argument needed here’

proof.text:
By hypothesis $H^i(L)$ is projective. Lift its identity along $q_i:Z^i\to H^i(L)$, obtaining $s_i:H^i(L)\to Z^i$ with $q_is_i=1$. Then
$$B^i\oplus H^i(L)\longrightarrow Z^i,\quad(u,h)\longmapsto u+s_i(h)$$
has inverse $z\mapsto(z-s_iq_i(z),q_i(z))$. Therefore $B^i$ is a retract of $Z^i$ and is projective by step 2. The induction starts with the projective module $B^{b+1}=0$; applying step 3 and then this step for $i=b,b-1,\ldots,a$ gives all the chosen $t_i,s_i$ and proves that all cycles and boundaries are projective. Outside this finite interval all modules in question are zero, and take the unique zero splittings. This establishes the induction without assuming any cycle or boundary is projective before it is obtained.

source.place: paragraph beginning ‘We record the elementary splitting argument needed here’

proof.text:
Combining the displayed inverses gives an $R$-linear isomorphism
$$\alpha_i:B^i\oplus H^i(L)\oplus B^{i+1}\longrightarrow L^i,\qquad(u,h,c)\longmapsto u+s_i(h)+t_i(c).$$
Here $B^i$ and $Z^i$ are included in $L^i$. Its inverse sends $x$ to $(z-s_iq_i(z),q_i(z),p_i(x))$, with $z=x-t_ip_i(x)$. Since $d^i$ kills $B^i$ and $s_i(H^i(L))$, while $d^it_i(c)=c$ as an element of $B^{i+1}\subseteq L^{i+1}$, we have
$$\alpha_{i+1}^{-1}d^i\alpha_i(u,h,c)=(c,0,0).$$
Thus these degreewise isomorphisms commute with the differentials: they are an isomorphism of complexes from the complex with the displayed coordinates and differential to $L$.

source.place: paragraph beginning ‘We record the elementary splitting argument needed here’

proof.text: Let $S$ be the zero-differential complex with $S^i=H^i(L)$, and let $D_i$ have $B^{i+1}$ in degrees $i,i+1$, identity differential between them, and zero elsewhere. In degree $i$ the direct sum $S\oplus\bigoplus_jD_j$ has precisely the coordinates $B^i\oplus H^i(L)\oplus B^{i+1}$, coming respectively from $D_{i-1},S,D_i$. Its differential is exactly $(u,h,c)\mapsto(c,0,0)$. Step 5 therefore proves the asserted complex isomorphism. All these sums are finite: $H^i(L)=0$ outside $[a,b]$ and $B^{i+1}=0$ unless $a\leq i<b$. Under the shift convention of [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], $H^i(L)[-i]$ is the single-term complex in degree $i$, so $S=\bigoplus_i H^i(L)[-i]$.

source.place: paragraph beginning ‘We record the elementary splitting argument needed here’

proof.text: For each $D_i$ define the degree $-1$ map $h_i^{i+1}:D_i^{i+1}\to D_i^i$ to be the identity of $B^{i+1}$ and all its other components to be zero. In degree $i$, $(dh_i+h_id)^i=h_i^{i+1}d^i=1$; in degree $i+1$, $(dh_i+h_id)^{i+1}=d^ih_i^{i+1}=1$; elsewhere both sides are zero. This proves contractibility with the convention stated in the item, including when $B^{i+1}=0$. Taking the finite direct sum of these homotopies contracts the disk summand. No assertion that an arbitrary acyclic complex is contractible is used.

source.place: paragraph beginning ‘We record the elementary splitting argument needed here’

proof.text: Projection $S\oplus\bigoplus_iD_i\to S$ is a chain map. In the coordinates of step 5 the cycles in degree $i$ are $(u,h,0)$ and the boundaries are precisely $(u,0,0)$: every $u\in B^i$ occurs as the third coordinate in degree $i-1$. Projection consequently induces the identity on the quotient $H^i(L)$ in every degree, so it is a quasi-isomorphism. Compose projection with the inverse of the complex isomorphism of step 5. The localization defining $D(R)$ in [def-weil-abstract-derived-category] inverts this quasi-isomorphism, giving $Q(L)\simeq Q(S)$. Finally $Q$ is an additive functor (the additive structure of $D(R)$ in [def-weil-abstract-derived-category] is the one induced from complexes), so it carries the finite direct sum $S=\bigoplus_iH^i(L)[-i]$ of complexes to the direct sum $\bigoplus_iQ(H^i(L)[-i])$ in $D(R)$, and $Q$ commutes with the shifts by the same node, so $Q(H^i(L)[-i])\simeq Q(H^i(L))[-i]$. This gives $L\simeq\bigoplus_iH^i(L)[-i]$ in $D(R)$. Only the finitely many degrees in $[a,b]$ contribute nonzero summands.
